opus-5.5.text:
I find it pretty plausible, though I'd frame it a bit carefully. The interesting question isn't really "does vision or video help the model see better," because obviously it does. It's whether training on non-language data transfers to the core reasoning ability, whether it makes the model a better thinker in general.

My intuition is that there's real signal there, but it's probably not where the bulk of the reasoning gains come from. Language is an incredibly compressed representation of human thought. A huge fraction of the useful structure of the world has already been distilled into text by people who spent their lives figuring it out. So per token, text is extraordinarily information-dense for reasoning in a way raw pixels or audio just aren't.

That said, there are things text underspecifies. Physical intuition is a good example: how objects move, how forces interact, spatial relationships. Humans learn a ton of that before we ever learn to talk, and it plausibly scaffolds a lot of our abstract reasoning. When you think about a math problem, you often visualize it. Geometric and spatial intuition sneaks into all kinds of supposedly abstract domains. So if a model builds a richer world model from video, it seems reasonable that some of that leaks into how it reasons about everything else.

The other angle I find compelling is that non-language data can be a source of grounded feedback. A lot of what makes reinforcement learning work well is having a verifiable signal: did the code run, did the proof check out. The physical world is the ultimate verifier. If models are interacting with environments, robotics, simulations, and learning from what actually happens rather than from what someone wrote about what happens, that's a qualitatively different kind of learning signal. You're not bounded by the ceiling of human-written descriptions.

Where I'd be skeptical is the idea that you just throw a mountain of YouTube into pretraining and reasoning magically jumps. The transfer results I'm aware of tend to be modest. Positive transfer between modalities seems to exist, especially at large scale, but it's not some dramatic unlock. I think the bigger lever for reasoning right now is RL on top of strong base models, letting them think for longer and get feedback on whether they're right.

So my overall take: likely helpful, probably more important for things like agency, embodiment, and grounded understanding than for pure abstract reasoning in the near term. But I wouldn't be surprised if, as we scale up multimodal and interactive training, we discover the transfer is bigger than we thought, because that's been the recurring lesson. Things that seem like they shouldn't generalize often do, once you have enough scale.

r001.rationale: It says video can build a richer world model and specifically identifies physical and spatial intuition as a plausible scaffold for broader reasoning.

r002.rationale: It does not report that fine-tuning on math problems improves entity recognition.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's very plausible, and honestly I think it's one of the more underrated ideas right now. If you look at what language gave us, it was this incredibly dense, pre-compressed representation of the world. Humans had already done a lot of the work of abstracting things into concepts and relationships, so the models got to learn from the distilled version. That's why language was the thing that worked first.

But language is also a bottleneck. There's a huge amount of structure in the world that nobody ever bothered to write down, either because it's too obvious to us or because it's hard to verbalize. Physical intuition, how objects move and deform, how a chemical process unfolds over time, what a protein actually does when it folds. If a model can learn directly from video, from simulation, from sensor data, it gets access to regularities that aren't in the text corpus at all.

The question I keep coming back to is whether that actually improves reasoning, or whether it just improves knowledge. And my intuition is that it does both, but the reasoning gains are the subtle part. A lot of what we call reasoning is really the ability to run a good internal model forward and check it against reality. If your world model is richer, your predictions are better, and your chains of thought have more to push against. You stop making the kinds of errors that come from only ever having seen descriptions of things rather than the things themselves.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking the data alone does it. Raw video is incredibly redundant and low in information per token compared to text. You need the right objective, and probably you need the model to be acting in some way, so it's learning what matters rather than everything. The RL side of this is where I'd expect the real leverage. Give a model a feedback loop against the physical or simulated world, and the non-language data stops being passive and starts being something it can actually learn to reason over.

So yes, plausible, and I'd bet on it mattering a lot over the next few years. It's just that the hard part isn't gathering the data, it's figuring out what to make the model do with it.

r001.rationale: The response calls reasoning gains from non-language data plausible and specifically describes learning physical intuition and world dynamics from video, simulation, and sensor data.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention fine-tuning on math problems or improving entity recognition.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s quite plausible. Language contains an enormous amount of information about the world, but it’s information that’s already been filtered through what humans find useful to describe. There’s a lot we know how to do that we don’t articulate very well.

Take watching someone manipulate an unfamiliar object. You can learn something about its geometry, what parts move, and what happens when you apply force, without anyone explaining it. To predict that sequence well, a model might need to develop representations of objects and causality that are useful beyond predicting the next frame.

The question is how much that transfers. Getting better at video prediction doesn’t automatically mean getting better at mathematical reasoning. You’d want to distinguish learning additional facts about the world from learning more general mechanisms for reasoning.

I’m particularly interested in interaction, where you can take an action and observe the result. That lets you test hypotheses instead of just observing correlations. It seems plausible that learning to do that across lots of environments could teach something useful about planning and correcting mistakes. But I’d treat the breadth of that transfer as an empirical question.

r001.rationale: The response says learning from video and interaction could teach models about geometry, motion, forces, causality, and planning, and calls this plausible for improving reasoning.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention fine-tuning on math problems or improved entity recognition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very plausible. Language contains a huge amount of information about the world, but it’s information that humans have already compressed into descriptions. If you watch something happen, you can learn relationships that nobody thought to write down.

Imagine watching an object fall, bounce, and come to rest. To predict that well across lots of different situations, you need some representation of how objects behave. And if you can act in the world, you get an even richer signal: you can try something and see whether your prediction was right.

The question is how much that transfers to the reasoning we care about. Getting better at predicting video doesn’t automatically mean getting better at proving a theorem. But I’d expect some shared capabilities—tracking a situation, understanding cause and effect, predicting the consequences of an action—to benefit. So I’d be surprised if language were the only useful source of training data for reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says learning from observation and interaction with the world is very plausible, using object motion and cause-and-effect prediction as examples of useful capabilities for reasoning.
